title: Backtracking Candidate Elimination: A One-Pass Algorithm for the Chip Testing Problem
summary: The paper studies the chip testing problem: n chips with a strict majority good, two-sided tests, adversarial bad chips, and the goal of identifying one guaranteed-good chip. It introduces Backtracking Candidate Elimination (BCE), a one-pass sequential algorithm that keeps a current candidate and a stack of retained chips, discarding the candidate and incoming chip on an inconsistent test and backtracking to the most recently retained chip. The paper proves that BCE returns a good chip using at most n−1 tests in O(n) time, illustrates it on GGBBBGG returning x7 after four tests, and relates it to Boyer–Moore majority voting.

claims.statement: On the 7-chip instance with hidden types G,G,B,B,B,G,G in scan order, BCE returns the good chip x7 after exactly 4 two-sided tests.
claims.metric: number of tests to return x7
claims.table_ref: Table 2, row i=7, result column and Section 4 example
claims.config_for_value: Algorithm 1 without early termination; chips x1..x7 have types G,G,B,B,B,G,G; two-sided Test(p,xi); bad verdicts may be arbitrary but every test in this trace is inconsistent regardless of the bad chip's answer.
claims.quote: The candidate backtracks from x1 to the retained chip x2, and BCE returns the good chip x7 after four tests.

claims.statement: In Algorithm 1, each chip is tested at most once as the incoming chip; it may later be used as the candidate in further tests.
claims.metric: maximum number of times a chip is the incoming chip in a test
claims.dataset: all valid input sequences (theorem for arbitrary n)
claims.split: all n and all strict-majority type assignments
claims.config_for_value: Algorithm 1; loop over i=2..n; each xi is the incoming chip in at most the single Test(p,xi) call at iteration i.
claims.est_compute: CPU, exhaustive check for n<=8 in seconds to minutes
claims.quote: Each chip is tested at most once as the incoming chip, although it may later serve as the candidate in further tests.

match_target.why: The central guarantee is the symbolic n−1 worst-case bound; C1 is the paper's only concrete end-to-end trace of that guarantee, exercising retain, discard/backtrack, and restart while returning x7 with 4 <= 7−1 tests. It is cheaper than exhaustive verification and still exercises the full Algorithm 1 control flow.

tolerance.why: Rule 4: a test count is an unbounded integer, so use 10% relative; 10% of 4 is 0.4 tests, which for an integer count means the implementation must use exactly 4 tests and return x7. Output identity x7 is categorical and must match.

requirements.stmt: Assume the input satisfies the strict-majority promise g > b; otherwise the correctness theorem does not apply and p=⊥ can expose a broken promise.
requirements.quote: Given the promise that strictly more than n/2 of the chips are good

requirements.stmt: Implement two-sided tests Test(x,y) that return an ordered pair of verdicts; a good chip's verdict is correct and a bad chip's verdict may be arbitrary and adaptive.
requirements.quote: A good chip always reports correctly. A bad chip may report anything, and we assume the bad chips collude adversarially.

requirements.stmt: Classify a test as consistent only when the returned pair is (G,G); every other pair is inconsistent.
requirements.quote: We say a test is consistent if it returns (G, G) and inconsistent otherwise.

requirements.stmt: On a consistent Test(p,xi), retain xi by pushing it onto R and keep p as the candidate, using Fact 1 that consistent chips have the same type.
requirements.quote: If Test(p, xi) returns (G, G), then p and xi have the same type

requirements.stmt: On an inconsistent Test(p,xi), discard both p and xi as a pair; Fact 2 guarantees the pair contains at least one bad chip.
requirements.quote: Otherwise, {p, xi} contains a bad chip, and both are discarded.

requirements.stmt: After discarding on an inconsistent test, backtrack: if R is nonempty, pop the most recently retained chip and make it the new candidate; otherwise set p=⊥.
requirements.quote: If R is nonempty, the most recently retained chip is popped and becomes the new candidate.

requirements.stmt: If p=⊥ when a new chip arrives, make that chip the candidate without performing a test.
requirements.quote: Case 1. No candidate (p = ⊥). Make xi the candidate without testing it.

requirements.stmt: Initialize p=x1 and R empty, then scan i=2..n once from left to right.
requirements.quote: Initially p = x1 and R is empty. When chip xi arrives:

requirements.stmt: After the scan, return the current candidate p; under the promise this chip is guaranteed good.
requirements.quote: At the end of the scan, BCE returns p.

requirements.stmt: Count tests as calls to Test(p,xi) only; perform at most one such call per loop iteration, giving at most n−1 tests total.
requirements.quote: BCE performs at most n −1 tests and runs in O(n) time.

requirements.stmt: Maintain the two invariants used in the proof: all retained chips have the same type, and every discarded pair is bad-heavy (at least as many bad as good).
requirements.quote: the retained chips form a homogeneous set (Lemma 3), and discarded chips are bad-heavy (Lemma 4).

requirements.stmt: If implementing the optional early-termination rule, after processing xi compute h=|Ci| and r=n−i; if h≥r and h≥1, stop and return p.
requirements.quote: If h ≥r and h ≥1, then every chip in Ci is good.

requirements.stmt: If implementing the one-directional variant, ask the incoming chip about the top of the stack; push on a good verdict, otherwise pop and discard both; return the bottom chip.
requirements.quote: a stack-based scan still finds a good chip with at most n −1 directed tests.

data.how_to_get: Hard-code the seven chips in scan order as G,G,B,B,B,G,G and run Algorithm 1; Table 2 expects output x7 after four tests.

data.name: Exhaustive valid chip configurations
data.how_to_get: For n=1..8, enumerate every length-n G/B string with more G than B; for each test, branch over every verdict pair allowed by Table 1, including adaptive bad-chip answers, and check the algorithm returns a good chip with at most n−1 tests on every branch.
